title: Checking more than one case
idea: One passing case isn't always enough. Checking a few examples gives you more confidence.

exercises.prompt: Why might you check more than one example?
options: To be more sure the program is right, not just lucky once
exercises.explanation: Passing once could be luck. A few passing cases give you real confidence the program behaves correctly.

exercises.prompt: If you check two different cases and both pass, you can be more confident than after just one.
exercises.explanation: More passing cases, more confidence. Each case that matches its expected output is more evidence it works.

exercises.prompt: Case 1 passes. Case 2 fails. What is the overall verdict?
options: Fail — a program must pass all its cases
exercises.explanation: If any case fails, the program isn't fully correct yet. It needs to pass every case you check.

exercises.prompt: You have a program that greets a name. You check it with 'Sam' and it passes. What's a good next move?
options: Check it with a different name too
exercises.explanation: Trying a second, different example (like 'Mai') checks that it works in general, not just for 'Sam'.

exercises.prompt: Re-checking with a fresh example helps prove the program isn't just right by accident.
exercises.explanation: A fresh example is a new test. If it passes too, your confidence grows that the program is truly correct.

exercises.prompt: You ran 3 cases. Case 1: pass. Case 2: pass. Case 3: fail. Which statements are true? (pick all)
exercises.explanation: Case 3 failed, so overall it's a fail, and case 3 is where to look. Not all three passed.

exercises.prompt: Put the multi-case checking steps in order.
blocks: Decide the expected output for each case
Run each case and read its real output
Compare each case and judge overall pass or fail
exercises.explanation: Know each expected output, run each case, then compare them all. Any fail makes the whole thing a fail.

exercises.prompt: Match each set of case results to the overall verdict.
exercises.explanation: All pass = pass. Any fail = fail. If you haven't checked, you don't know yet.

exercises.prompt: Checking many cases is overkill for every tiny program.
exercises.explanation: Even small programs benefit from a second case. It catches 'lucky once' bugs with almost no extra effort.

exercises.prompt: What's the real goal of checking several cases?
options: Confidence that the program works in general, not just for one input
exercises.explanation: The point is confidence. More passing cases means you can trust the program across different inputs.
